items.description: Analyze repository structure and existing infrastructure
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce a written document (in results/) listing all modules, files, and their purposes, including the semantic_scholar.py tool, figures/ and results/ directories, and how the orchestration framework connects them. Must cover at least 5 distinct components.

items.description: Conduct comprehensive web search for state-of-the-art SSSP algorithms and recent breakthroughs
items.acceptance_criteria: Search the web for papers from STOC, FOCS, SODA, and ESA (2022-2026) on SSSP improvements. Must identify and summarize at least 8 key results including: Fredman-Tarjan 1987, Thorup 1999, Bernstein-Nanongkai-Wulff-Nilsen (FOCS 2022), Bringmann-Cassis-Fischer (FOCS 2023), Duan-Mao-Mao-Shu-Yin (STOC 2025), Haeupler et al. universal optimality (FOCS 2024), Fineman (STOC 2024), and Huang-Jin-Quanrud (SODA 2025). Write a structured summary in results/literature_review.md.

items.description: Create and populate sources.bib with BibTeX entries for all consulted sources
items.acceptance_criteria: Create sources.bib in the repo root containing valid BibTeX entries for at least 12 relevant papers. Must include entries for Fredman-Tarjan 1987, Thorup 1999, Bernstein-Nanongkai-Wulff-Nilsen 2022, Bringmann-Cassis-Fischer 2023, Duan et al. STOC 2025, Haeupler et al. FOCS 2024, Fineman STOC 2024, and Fakcharoenphol-Rao 2001. Use semantic_scholar.py or web search to obtain accurate citation metadata. Each entry must have author, title, year, and venue fields.

items.description: Formalize the complexity landscape and identify exploitable gaps
items.acceptance_criteria: Write a technical note (results/complexity_gaps.md) containing: (1) a table of current best bounds for SSSP across graph families (directed/undirected, real/integer weights, non-negative/negative, planar, bounded treewidth, DAGs), (2) identification of at least 3 specific gaps between upper and lower bounds, and (3) analysis of which gaps are most promising for improvement. Must cite at least 6 papers from sources.bib.

items.description: Analyze the Duan et al. recursive frontier reduction and interval-pivot mechanism
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce a detailed technical summary (results/duan_analysis.md) of the STOC 2025 and 2026 algorithms by Duan et al., covering: (1) the interval-pivot mechanism, (2) the Bounded Multi-Source Shortest Path (BMSSP) subroutine, (3) how they bypass the sorting barrier, (4) their practical limitations (crossover at ~10^67 vertices), and (5) potential avenues for extending or improving these techniques. At least 2000 words.

items.description: Survey conditional lower bounds and identify proof barriers for SSSP
items.acceptance_criteria: Write results/lower_bounds.md documenting: (1) why no super-linear unconditional lower bound exists for SSSP, (2) the sorting barrier and how it was bypassed, (3) Haeupler et al.'s universal optimality result and its implications, (4) the OMv hypothesis and SETH-based barriers for dynamic SSSP, and (5) what constraints these place on possible approaches. Must cite at least 4 specific results from sources.bib.

items.description: Implement Dijkstra's algorithm with Fibonacci heap achieving O(m + n log n)
items.acceptance_criteria: Working Python implementation of Dijkstra + Fibonacci heap in src/baselines/dijkstra_fib.py. Must correctly compute shortest paths on directed graphs with non-negative real weights. Include unit tests in tests/test_dijkstra.py covering: (1) empty graph, (2) single vertex, (3) complete graph K_10, (4) graph with parallel edges, (5) disconnected graph. All tests pass.

items.description: Implement graph generators for diverse graph families
items.acceptance_criteria: Create src/generators/graphs.py with functions to generate: (1) Erdos-Renyi random directed graphs G(n, p), (2) random sparse graphs with m = O(n), (3) random dense graphs with m = Theta(n^2), (4) grid/lattice graphs, (5) planar graphs, (6) graphs with bounded treewidth, (7) scale-free (power-law) graphs. Each generator must accept n (vertices) and return an adjacency list with real-valued non-negative weights. Include tests in tests/test_generators.py verifying edge counts and connectivity properties.

items.description: Build a benchmarking and profiling framework
items.acceptance_criteria: Create src/benchmark.py that: (1) runs a given SSSP algorithm on a specified graph, (2) measures wall-clock time, number of comparisons, number of decrease-key operations, and memory usage, (3) supports multiple trials with mean/stddev reporting, (4) outputs results as JSON to results/benchmarks/. Include a CLI interface accepting algorithm name, graph type, and size parameters. Demonstrate with at least 3 runs of Dijkstra on graphs of size n=1000, 5000, 10000.

items.description: Profile Dijkstra baseline and identify computational bottlenecks
items.acceptance_criteria: Run the benchmarking framework on Dijkstra+Fibonacci heap across 5 graph types (sparse random, dense random, grid, planar, scale-free) at sizes n=1000, 5000, 10000, 50000. Produce results/profiling_report.md with: (1) runtime scaling plots saved in figures/, (2) breakdown of time spent in decrease-key vs delete-min vs graph traversal, (3) identification of the dominant cost component for each graph type, (4) comparison of empirical scaling against theoretical O(m + n log n). At least 3 figures generated.

items.description: Implement reference algorithms for comparison: Bellman-Ford and binary-heap Dijkstra
items.acceptance_criteria: Implement in src/baselines/: (1) bellman_ford.py for Bellman-Ford O(mn) algorithm, (2) dijkstra_binary.py for Dijkstra with binary heap O((m+n) log n). Both must pass the same test suite as Dijkstra+Fibonacci heap. Benchmark both on the same graph instances from item_010 and add comparative timings to results/profiling_report.md.

items.description: Identify a target graph family or weight model where current bounds leave room for improvement
items.acceptance_criteria: Write results/target_selection.md with: (1) a ranked list of at least 4 candidate targets (e.g., sparse directed graphs m=O(n log n), bounded-genus graphs, graphs with bounded highway dimension, directed graphs with small nesting width), (2) for each candidate: current best bound, gap to linear time, and feasibility assessment, (3) a justified selection of one primary target with a specific conjectured improvement. Must reference findings from the literature review and cite at least 5 papers from sources.bib.

items.description: Design a novel algorithmic approach for the selected target
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce results/algorithm_design.md containing: (1) a high-level description of the proposed algorithm, (2) pseudocode with at most 50 lines, (3) identification of the key technical insight that enables improvement (e.g., structure-aware decomposition, new priority queue design, relaxed ordering), (4) informal argument for why the approach should achieve the claimed complexity, (5) comparison with at least 3 prior approaches (Dijkstra, Thorup, Duan et al.) explaining the distinction. At least 3000 words.

items.description: Develop a formal complexity analysis of the proposed algorithm
items.acceptance_criteria: Write results/complexity_proof.md with: (1) formal statement of the claimed theorem (time and space bounds), (2) lemmas with proofs for each major subroutine, (3) a complete proof of the main theorem composing subroutine bounds, (4) analysis of correctness (the algorithm produces valid shortest paths), (5) identification of any assumptions or restrictions (e.g., comparison-addition model, word-RAM, specific graph family). Each lemma and theorem must have explicit proof. Must cite relevant prior techniques from sources.bib.

items.description: Implement the proposed algorithm
items.acceptance_criteria: Working implementation in src/novel/algorithm.py. Must: (1) correctly compute SSSP on the target graph family, verified by comparison with Dijkstra on 100 random instances of sizes n=100, 1000, 10000, (2) pass all correctness tests in tests/test_novel.py, (3) include instrumentation for counting comparisons, decrease-key operations, and other relevant metrics, (4) handle edge cases (empty graph, single vertex, disconnected graphs).

items.description: Explore a secondary approach: structure-exploiting priority queue or decomposition technique
items.acceptance_criteria: Document in results/secondary_approach.md: (1) description of an alternative algorithmic idea distinct from the primary approach, (2) analysis of its potential complexity advantage, (3) assessment of whether it complements or competes with the primary approach, (4) either a proof sketch of its bounds or a concrete argument for why it does not achieve the target. At least 1500 words. If the secondary approach proves superior, update the primary approach accordingly.

items.description: Run systematic experiments comparing the novel algorithm against baselines on synthetic graphs
items.acceptance_criteria: Execute benchmarks on the target graph family at sizes n = 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000 with at least 5 trials each. Compare the novel algorithm against Dijkstra+Fibonacci heap and Dijkstra+binary heap. Record: wall-clock time, number of comparisons, and memory. Save raw results as JSON in results/benchmarks/synthetic/. Produce at least 4 scaling plots in figures/ showing runtime vs n, comparisons vs n, runtime vs m, and speedup ratio.

items.description: Test the novel algorithm on real-world graph datasets
items.acceptance_criteria: Download or generate at least 3 real-world directed graph datasets (e.g., road networks from DIMACS, social network subgraphs, web graphs). Run the novel algorithm and Dijkstra baseline on each. Report results in results/real_world_results.md with timing comparisons and a discussion of how graph structure affects performance. At least 2 figures in figures/.

items.description: Perform ablation studies and sensitivity analysis
items.acceptance_criteria: In results/ablation.md, document experiments varying: (1) graph density (m/n ratio from 1.5 to n), (2) weight distribution (uniform, exponential, heavy-tailed), (3) any algorithm-specific parameters (e.g., decomposition depth, bucket sizes). For each variable, produce a plot in figures/ showing its effect on runtime. Identify which factors most strongly affect the novel algorithm's advantage over baselines. At least 3 ablation experiments with corresponding figures.

items.description: Statistical validation of experimental results
items.acceptance_criteria: Compute and report in results/statistical_validation.md: (1) mean, median, standard deviation, and 95% confidence intervals for all runtime measurements, (2) paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing the novel algorithm vs each baseline on matched graph instances, (3) regression analysis fitting empirical runtime to predicted complexity curves (e.g., f(n) = c * n * log^a(n)), (4) R-squared values for curve fits. All p-values must be reported; improvements must be statistically significant (p < 0.05) on at least 3 graph sizes.

items.description: Compare results against complexity claims from prior work identified in the literature review
items.acceptance_criteria: Write results/prior_work_comparison.md comparing the novel algorithm's empirical and theoretical performance against at least 5 prior results from sources.bib. For each comparison: state the prior bound, state the new bound or empirical finding, and explain whether the novel approach achieves an improvement and under what conditions. Include a summary table of complexities.

items.description: Write the main research report
items.acceptance_criteria: Create results/research_report.md with sections: (1) Abstract (200 words), (2) Introduction and motivation citing the 40-year O(m + n log n) barrier, (3) Related Work summarizing at least 10 papers from sources.bib, (4) Algorithm Description with pseudocode, (5) Complexity Analysis with formal theorem statement and proof sketch, (6) Experimental Results with embedded figure references, (7) Discussion of practical implications, (8) Conclusion and Open Problems. Total length at least 5000 words.

items.description: Generate publication-quality figures
items.acceptance_criteria: Produce at least 6 final figures in figures/ using matplotlib or similar: (1) complexity landscape table/diagram, (2) runtime scaling log-log plot with fitted curves, (3) speedup ratio plot (novel vs Dijkstra), (4) comparison count scaling plot, (5) ablation heatmap or multi-panel plot, (6) real-world dataset performance bar chart. All figures must have labeled axes, legends, and titles. Save as both PNG and PDF.

items.description: Document limitations, failure modes, and threats to validity
items.acceptance_criteria: Write results/limitations.md covering: (1) graph families where the novel approach does NOT improve over Dijkstra, (2) constant-factor overhead and practical crossover points, (3) model assumptions (comparison-addition vs word-RAM), (4) threats to validity of experimental results (machine variability, implementation quality, generator bias), (5) comparison with the Haeupler et al. universal optimality result to clarify what is and isn't being claimed. At least 1500 words.

items.description: Write future work roadmap and identify open problems
items.acceptance_criteria: Create results/future_work.md with: (1) at least 3 specific open problems arising from this research, (2) proposed next steps for extending the result (e.g., to broader graph families, negative weights, dynamic settings), (3) potential connections to parallel/distributed SSSP, (4) assessment of whether the approach could eventually lead to O(m + n) SSSP for general directed graphs. Must cite at least 3 recent papers from sources.bib as motivation for future directions.
